Pixel Blade · Warrior · the Ninja

He is losing resolution.

Fine speckle against the cloth, coarsening to chunky blocks far out. Not shedding particles — losing definition.

MUCH smaller, finer pixels close to the body, and getting larger, lower-res as they dissolve further from the body.

Spencer Lee

The gradient

Uniform blocks read as confetti.

The first pass used one block size throughout, and it read as an effect — particles coming off a man. Growing the blocks as they travel changes what the image is saying: he is not shedding pieces, he is losing definition, and the further a block gets the less of him it remembers.

A block is redrawn at the size of where it LANDS

Not where it came from — so travelling further coarsens it further. That single detail is what makes the falloff feel like a physical process instead of a scatter.

--b0 4 --b1 48 --bk 1.7 at 2K. If the fine end gets too large the gradient disappears and it goes straight back to confetti.

The medium

Ink is theirs. Pixels are his.

Forcing one dissolution medium across all three figures is what cost the coherence. The fix is that the medium is per-figure — and the split is the same arc the whole brand runs on.

It was in the name

Pixel Blade. And on record since round two — "blades are no longer steel. Pixels." The ancient figures come apart in ink, the modern one in pixels. It should not have taken four rounds to find, and Monk and Samurai stay exactly as they were.

How it is actually made

In code, not by generation.

Four generation attempts put the pixels beside him — a field on the wall next to an intact character. Image models read this as an adjacent object every time, the same failure the ink had.

brand/pixelate.py

Blocks the band, removes blocks with probability rising toward the outer edge, fills the holes with clean background copied from a column outside the figure, then redraws a fraction of what came loose at a rising offset with density falling away.

  • The edge is genuinely chewed, not suggested.
  • Every block is provably a piece of the cloth it left — the colour is sampled, not invented.
  • Deterministic. Same seed, same result — which is what a design system needs and a lucky generation can never give.
  • It is the site animation too. The same algorithm runs in canvas.

  • Square, large, flat

    Hard right angles, solid colour, no anti-aliasing, no rotation, no blur. A 16-bit sprite edge — smaller reads as noise, larger as damage. 24–30px at 2K.

  • One side only

    The side nearest a wall or shadow. The other side stays completely intact with a clean unbroken outline.

  • No gap

    The loose squares begin exactly where the cloth ends.

  • Up and out

    As if lifted on a breeze from below. Densest at the edge, thinning as they rise, many lost in the shadow they drift into.

  • Cloth colour

    Bone, sand, grey, charcoal, black. They do not glow. At most one or two in a hundred carry the cyan of the plating beneath.

  • Never

    Smoke, mist, ink, tendrils, embers, sparks. And never glitch art — no RGB splitting, scan lines, chromatic aberration or holograms.

The last of the skin

The plating runs into the collar.

Below the jaw guard, a gorget of overlapping segmented plates wraps the whole throat in the same faceted language — seam lines visible, running without interruption into the high collar. Mask and gorget read as one continuous machined piece.

No jaw, no chin, no cheek, no ear, and above all no throat. Hands may be bare; the neck may not.

Two traps, both hit while fixing this

1. Cyan hair keeps coming back. Teal strands reappeared at the temples twice after being told not to — the generator adds them as a stylistic reflex. Ban it by colour as well as by noun.

2. Neck armour creeps into a mecha suit. Asking for throat plating produced a full armoured torso with a glowing chest orb, and the parka and hood vanished entirely. Always bound it: armour limited to head and throat, everything below the collar is cloth — a person in heavy streetwear wearing a helmet, not a robot.

Register

The stillness is the threat.

Not the hero of the scene — the thing that already happened. Rumour that turns out to have been true, and everything about him in past tense.

Adaptive colour

He is the day/night switch.

Light enough to vanish into a crowd, dark when he needs to be. Measured across the same garment, the same silhouette swings from value ~76% to ~19%.

Light · blending

Standing at the mouth of the alley — the only shadow available on a bright street, and he is already half into it.

Dark · working

Same garment, same cut. Signage kept near-grey so he is the only lit thing.

Useful beyond the fiction

He does in one figure what the site does across pages — the natural transition device between the light pages and the dark ones. The only element that belongs to both modes at once and changes by choice rather than by placement.

Mechanics

Modern meets ancient.

  • A helmet, not a face

    Faceted plating over the whole head with lit cyan channels or a glowing optic, continuing into a segmented gorget at the throat. No skin above the collar. No hair of any colour. Below the collar, cloth only.

  • Layered and long

    Parka hem well below the hip toward the knee, worn open over an offset mid-layer, a high-collared under-layer and stacked cargo. Each hem at a different length. Never cropped — the bulk is the silhouette.

  • Reads young

    Lighter build, casual weight, unhurried posture.

  • No drawn weapon

    A cybernetic arm instead. He has not needed one across six plates — his hands are the weapon.

  • Desaturated Tokyo

    Signage dim and near-grey, never a neon blaze. The city stays dark so he can be the only lit thing.

  • Kindle, hairline

    Narrow cyan channels at 0.4–1.0% of frame coverage. --pb-kindle marks what is not proven yet — and a myth qualifies.
